metadata.source: RBI Glossary, Indian Banks' Association (IBA), Bank Management Standards

terms.statutory_definition: The proportion of a commercial bank's total deposits that are held in current accounts and savings accounts.
terms.simple_explanation: Current and savings accounts offer very low or zero interest. A higher CASA ratio means the bank gets very cheap money from customers, making lending far more profitable.
terms.exam_relevance: Frequently asked in Mains exams: higher CASA = higher net interest margins and lower cost of funds.
terms.trap_alert: Don't confuse CASA with Term Deposits (FD/RD). Term deposits are high-cost funds, while CASA are low-cost demand deposits.
terms.example: If Bank X has ₹100 Crore in total deposits, and ₹45 Crore is in Savings + Current accounts, its CASA ratio is 45%.
terms.pyq_frequency: Very High (Asked 6+ times in SBI/IBPS Mains)

terms.statutory_definition: Ratio of a bank's regulatory capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) to its total risk-weighted assets, mandated under Basel III norms.
terms.simple_explanation: A financial health safety cushion. It measures how much loss-absorbing capital a bank holds relative to the riskiness of the loans it has given out.
terms.exam_relevance: RBI mandates a minimum CRAR of 9% for Scheduled Commercial Banks (11.5% including Capital Conservation Buffer CCB), and 12% for Public Sector Banks.
terms.trap_alert: Basel III global minimum is 8%, but RBI prescribes a stricter minimum of 9% in India.
terms.example: If a bank has ₹9 Crore of regulatory capital against ₹100 Crore of risk-weighted assets, its CRAR is 9%.

terms.statutory_definition: Bank assets or off-balance sheet exposures, weighted according to their relative risk of default and market loss as per RBI guidelines.
terms.simple_explanation: Not all loans are equally risky. A loan to the Government of India has 0% risk weight, a home loan has ~35-50% risk weight, while an unsecured credit card loan has 125-150% risk weight.
terms.exam_relevance: Used in denominator of CRAR: CRAR = Regulatory Capital / Total Risk-Weighted Assets.
terms.trap_alert: Cash and Central Government Securities have ZERO percent (0%) risk weight under RBI norms.
terms.example: A ₹100 Crore investment in G-Secs contributes ₹0 to RWA, but ₹100 Crore in unsecured loans contributes ₹125-150 Crore to RWA.

terms.statutory_definition: The highest quality core equity capital of a bank comprising paid-up equity shares, statutory reserves, and general reserves.
terms.simple_explanation: The purest form of a bank's own money that absorbs unexpected losses immediately on a going-concern basis.
terms.exam_relevance: Under RBI Basel III rules, minimum CET1 is 5.5% of RWA (plus 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer = 8.0%).
terms.trap_alert: Minimum CET1 is 5.5% (RBI), while global Basel III minimum is 4.5%.
terms.example: Common stock capital and retained earnings.

terms.statutory_definition: Bank credit in India minus bills rediscounted with RBI and other approved financial institutions, plus investments in non-SLR bonds in HTM category.
terms.simple_explanation: The benchmark figure against which RBI calculates all Priority Sector Lending (PSL) percentage targets for commercial banks.
terms.exam_relevance: 40% of ANBC for Domestic Commercial Banks; 75% of ANBC for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Small Finance Banks (SFBs).
terms.trap_alert: PSL targets are calculated on ANBC or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is HIGHER.
terms.example: If a bank has ₹1,000 Crore ANBC, it must allocate at least ₹400 Crore to Priority Sectors.

terms.statutory_definition: Mandatory credit allocation prescribed by RBI to specified vital sectors of the economy that may otherwise struggle to access institutional credit.
terms.simple_explanation: Sectors mandated by RBI: (1) Agriculture, (2) MSME, (3) Export Credit, (4) Education, (5) Housing, (6) Social Infrastructure, (7) Renewable Energy, (8) Others/Weaker Sections.
terms.exam_relevance: Domestic SCBs: 40% overall (18% Agriculture with 10% for Small & Marginal Farmers, 7.5% Micro Enterprises, 12% Weaker Sections). Shortfall goes to RIDF (NABARD).
terms.trap_alert: Foreign banks with 20 branches and above have the SAME 40% target as domestic commercial banks.
terms.example: A bank buying PSLC to meet its agriculture sub-target deficit.
terms.pyq_frequency: Extremely High (Appears in almost every Mains exam)

terms.statutory_definition: A loan or an advance where interest and/or installment of principal remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days in respect of a term loan.
terms.simple_explanation: When a borrower stops paying EMI or interest for over 90 consecutive days, the loan stops earning revenue for the bank and is marked as an NPA.
terms.exam_relevance: For agricultural loans: overdue for 2 crop seasons (short duration crops) or 1 crop season (long duration crops).
terms.trap_alert: Don't say 90 days for agricultural loans! For agriculture, NPA is measured in 'Crop Seasons' (2 seasons for short duration, 1 season for long duration).
terms.example: Borrower fails to pay home loan installment from Jan 1 to March 31 (90 days). On Day 91, account becomes Substandard NPA.

terms.statutory_definition: An early-warning asset classification before an account formally turns into an NPA (0 to 90 days overdue).
terms.simple_explanation: SMA-0: 1 to 30 days overdue. SMA-1: 31 to 60 days overdue. SMA-2: 61 to 90 days overdue. Enables banks to spot distress early.
terms.exam_relevance: Questions test the exact day ranges of SMA-0, SMA-1, and SMA-2.
terms.trap_alert: SMA-1 is 31 to 60 days (NOT 1 to 30). SMA-0 is 1 to 30 days.
terms.example: A company missing its EMI payment for 45 days is tagged under SMA-1.

terms.statutory_definition: The ratio of provisioning set aside by a bank to its gross non-performing assets (Gross NPA).
terms.simple_explanation: Shows what percentage of bad loans has already been covered with safety provisions set aside from the bank's profit.
terms.exam_relevance: Formula: (Total Provisions held for NPAs / Gross NPAs) × 100. High PCR (> 70-80%) reflects robust balance-sheet health.
terms.trap_alert: Higher PCR is BETTER, whereas higher Net NPA is WORSE.
terms.example: If Gross NPA is ₹100 Crore and bank holds provisions of ₹75 Crore, PCR is 75%.

terms.statutory_definition: The difference between total interest earned by a bank on loans/investments and total interest paid on deposits/borrowings, divided by total average interest-earning assets.
terms.simple_explanation: The core profit margin of a commercial bank's lending business.
terms.exam_relevance: Formula: (Interest Earned - Interest Expended) / Average Earning Assets.
terms.trap_alert: NIM measures yield on earning assets, NOT overall net profit margin.
terms.example: Indian banks typically target a NIM of 3.0% to 4.0%.

terms.statutory_definition: A bank's operating costs (excluding provisions) expressed as a percentage of its operating income (Net Interest Income + Non-interest Income).
terms.simple_explanation: Measures operational efficiency. A lower ratio means the bank runs very lean and spends less money to generate revenue.
terms.exam_relevance: Unlike profitability metrics where higher is better, a LOWER Cost to Income ratio represents superior efficiency.
terms.trap_alert: Do NOT think higher is better here! Lower is more efficient.
terms.example: A bank spending ₹45 to earn ₹100 has a Cost-to-Income ratio of 45%.

terms.statutory_definition: The percentage of the total property value that a bank or housing finance company is permitted to lend.
terms.simple_explanation: If a house costs ₹1 Crore and RBI permits an LTV of 80%, the bank can give a maximum loan of ₹80 Lakh; borrower must pay ₹20 Lakh as down-payment (margin).
terms.exam_relevance: RBI caps LTV on housing loans: 90% for loans up to ₹30 Lakh, 80% for ₹30-75 Lakh, and 75% for loans above ₹75 Lakh.
terms.trap_alert: For housing loans above ₹75 Lakh, maximum permissible LTV is strictly 75%.
terms.example: A ₹25 Lakh loan on a ₹30 Lakh home equals an LTV of 83.3% (within 90% cap).

terms.statutory_definition: An account maintained by an Indian domestic bank with an overseas foreign bank in foreign currency.
terms.simple_explanation: State Bank of India opening and maintaining an account in US Dollars with JPMorgan Chase in New York.
terms.exam_relevance: Latin origin: Nostro means 'Ours' ('Our money in your bank').
terms.trap_alert: Do not confuse Nostro (Our account with you in foreign currency) with Vostro (Your account with us in Indian Rupees).
terms.example: SBI maintaining an account in Japanese Yen with Bank of Tokyo.
terms.pyq_frequency: Extremely High (Perennial favourite in Bank exams)

terms.statutory_definition: An account maintained by a foreign bank with an Indian domestic bank in domestic currency (Indian Rupees - INR).
terms.simple_explanation: Russia's Sberbank opening and maintaining an account in Indian Rupees with UCO Bank in Kolkata to settle rupee trade.
terms.exam_relevance: Latin origin: Vostro means 'Yours' ('Your money in our bank'). Used heavily for Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) for international trade.
terms.trap_alert: A Vostro account is held in the host nation's domestic currency (Rupees in India).
terms.example: Sberbank of Russia holding an INR account with IndusInd Bank.

terms.statutory_definition: An account held by a third-party bank with another bank, referred to by an entity acting as intermediary.
terms.simple_explanation: When Bank of Baroda tells Citibank New York to settle a payment using State Bank of India's Nostro account at Citibank: 'Their account with you'.
terms.exam_relevance: Latin: Loro means 'Their'. Used in three-party inter-bank settlements.
terms.trap_alert: Nostro = Ours; Vostro = Yours; Loro = Theirs.
terms.example: Bank A settles via Bank B's account at Bank C.

terms.full_form: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
terms.statutory_definition: A global member-owned cooperative and secure messaging network through which banks worldwide exchange standardized financial transaction messages.
terms.simple_explanation: SWIFT does NOT transfer actual funds; it securely transmits payment orders and instructions using standardized 8 or 11-character SWIFT / BIC codes.
terms.exam_relevance: Headquarters: La Hulpe (near Brussels), Belgium. Founded: 1973. Code length: 8 or 11 characters (Bank Code + Country Code + Location Code + optional Branch Code).
terms.trap_alert: SWIFT is a secure MESSAGING system, NOT a fund settlement clearinghouse.
terms.example: PUNBINBBXXX (Punjab National Bank SWIFT Code).

terms.statutory_definition: An 11-character alphanumeric code used to uniquely identify individual bank branches participating in electronic fund transfer systems (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS).
terms.simple_explanation: 11 characters breakdown: First 4 characters = Bank Name alphabets; 5th character = Reserved as ZERO '0'; Last 6 characters = Specific Branch numeric/alphanumeric code.
terms.exam_relevance: Crucial exam question: The 5th character of an IFSC is ALWAYS ZERO ('0').
terms.trap_alert: The 5th character is numeric '0' (zero), NOT the alphabet 'O'. Total length is exactly 11 characters.
terms.example: SBIN0001234 (First 4: SBIN = State Bank of India; 5th: 0; Last 6: 001234 = Branch code).

terms.statutory_definition: A 9-digit numeric code printed at the bottom of bank cheques (cheque band) using magnetic ink for automated cheque clearing under Cheque Truncation System (CTS).
terms.simple_explanation: 9 digits breakdown: First 3 digits = City Code (matching Postal PIN code first 3 digits); Middle 3 digits = Bank Code; Last 3 digits = Specific Branch Code.
terms.exam_relevance: Exam questions test what the first 3, middle 3, or last 3 digits represent.
terms.trap_alert: MICR is 9 digits (PURELY NUMERIC), while IFSC is 11 characters (ALPHANUMERIC).
terms.example: 110002001 (110 = Delhi City, 002 = SBI Bank, 001 = Main Branch).

terms.statutory_definition: A 20-digit globally unique alphanumeric reference code used to identify legally distinct legal entities that engage in financial transactions.
terms.simple_explanation: A global passport for corporations and financial entities, designed post-2008 global financial crisis to assess systemic corporate risk.
terms.exam_relevance: Length: exactly 20 digits. Mandated by RBI for all entities undertaking single payment transactions of ₹50 Crore and above via RTGS/NEFT.
terms.trap_alert: LEI length is 20 digits (NOT 11, NOT 16). Threshold for non-individual entities in RTGS/NEFT is ₹50 Crore.

terms.full_form: Marginal Cost of Funds Based Lending Rate
terms.statutory_definition: Internal benchmark interest rate for commercial banks introduced by RBI with effect from April 1, 2016, based on the marginal cost of borrowing funds.
terms.simple_explanation: Replaced the Base Rate system. Calculated based on 4 components: (1) Marginal cost of funds, (2) Negative carry on CRR, (3) Operating costs, (4) Tenor premium.
terms.exam_relevance: Introduced on April 1, 2016. Succeeded Base Rate. Later superseded by EBLR for retail loans from October 1, 2019.
terms.trap_alert: MCLR is an INTERNAL benchmark (each bank calculates its own). EBLR is linked to an EXTERNAL benchmark like RBI Repo Rate.
terms.example: 1-year MCLR for SBI set at 8.75%.

terms.statutory_definition: Lending rate mechanism made mandatory by RBI for all new floating rate retail loans (housing, auto) and MSME loans sanctioned by SCBs from October 1, 2019.
terms.simple_explanation: Banks must link floating retail loan interest rates to an external benchmark: (a) RBI Policy Repo Rate, or (b) 91-day / 182-day T-Bill yield, or (c) Any other benchmark published by FBIL.
terms.exam_relevance: Mandatory effective date: October 1, 2019. Ensures instantaneous transmission of RBI repo rate changes to borrowers.
terms.trap_alert: Banks are NOT allowed to adopt multiple benchmarks within the same loan category.
terms.example: SBI EBLR = Repo Rate (6.50%) + Spread/Margin (2.65%) = 9.15%.

terms.statutory_definition: An application mechanism developed by SEBI for applying to IPOs and Rights Issues where money remains blocked in the investor's own bank account until allotment.
terms.simple_explanation: Your money does NOT leave your bank account during an IPO bid. It is just locked/blocked. You earn savings interest on it until shares are allotted.
terms.exam_relevance: Introduced by SEBI. Self-Certified Syndicate Banks (SCSBs) provide ASBA service. Mandatory for retail public issues.
terms.trap_alert: Money is debited ONLY upon confirmed share allotment; otherwise the lien/block is simply removed.
terms.example: Applying for an IPO of ₹15,000 using UPI ASBA mandate.

terms.statutory_definition: The percentage difference between the book value of a debt owed to lenders and the actual amount the lenders agree to accept as settlement under a resolution plan.
terms.simple_explanation: If a bankrupt company owes banks ₹1,000 Crore, and banks accept ₹300 Crore to close the loan under IBC, the ₹700 Crore forgiven (70%) is the 'haircut'.
terms.exam_relevance: Frequently asked in context of IBC 2016 corporate debt resolutions.
terms.trap_alert: In collateral lending, haircut also refers to discount deducted from market value of pledged securities to guard against price fluctuations.
terms.example: Banks taking an 80% haircut on an insolvent steel mill.

terms.statutory_definition: A legally authorized temporary suspension, postponement, or grace period during which a borrower is not required to make scheduled EMI or principal payments.
terms.simple_explanation: A payment break granted during construction periods, education courses, or national crises (like COVID-19). Interest usually continues to accrue during the period.
terms.exam_relevance: Under Section 45 of Banking Regulation Act, RBI can recommend a moratorium on a distressed bank's operations to Central Government for up to 6 months.
terms.trap_alert: Moratorium is a DEFERRAL, not a loan waiver. Interest continues to accumulate during the moratorium.
terms.example: Education loan EMI begins 6 months to 1 year after course completion (the study duration is the moratorium).

terms.statutory_definition: An anomalous economic condition characterized by slow economic growth, high unemployment, and persistently high inflation all occurring at the same time.
terms.simple_explanation: The worst nightmare for a central bank. Normal cures for inflation (hiking rates) worsen unemployment, while curing unemployment (rate cuts) worsens inflation.
terms.exam_relevance: High exam probability: questions ask what combination defines stagflation (High Inflation + Stagnant Growth + High Unemployment).
terms.trap_alert: Deflation is falling prices. Stagflation is STAGNANT GDP growth combined with HIGH inflation.
terms.example: 1970s global oil crisis.

terms.statutory_definition: The excess of total government expenditure over total receipts (excluding borrowings) during a financial year.
terms.simple_explanation: How much money the Government of India needs to borrow in total to fund all its spending in that year.
terms.exam_relevance: Formula: Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts). FRBM Act targets 3.0% of GDP.
terms.trap_alert: Fiscal deficit EXCLUDES borrowings from total receipts (because the deficit ITSELF is what must be borrowed).
terms.example: India's fiscal deficit target for FY 2025-26 set at 4.5% of GDP.

terms.statutory_definition: The fiscal deficit of the current year minus interest payments on past borrowings.
terms.simple_explanation: Shows the government's borrowing requirement for current year expenditures alone, stripping out the burden of paying interest on old historical debts.
terms.exam_relevance: Formula: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments. When Primary Deficit is ZERO, Fiscal Deficit is equal to interest liabilities.
terms.trap_alert: Do not confuse Primary Deficit with Revenue Deficit! Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts.
terms.example: If Fiscal Deficit is ₹15 Lakh Crore and Interest Payments are ₹10 Lakh Crore, Primary Deficit is ₹5 Lakh Crore.
